newsitem.title: ISRAEL: In Washington, the meeting is the message.
newsitem.headline: In Washington, the meeting is the message.

text.p: At low points in the five-year roller coaster of the Middle East peace process the United States nudges Arabs and Israelis on to the world stage to show they are still talking.
The Israeli-PLO emergency summit in Washington this week is just such an occasion where the meeting will be the message, Middle East analysts and diplomats say.
The symbolism of summits and handshakes has proved as important as the substance of negotiations in seeking an end to the decades-old struggle between two peoples on one land.
There will be no serious negotiating in Washington, the sources said.
In the presence of their host President Bill Clinton, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat will politely agree to disagree.
"The real talking will be done back here in the Middle East at a follow-up summit, maybe in Egypt," a Western diplomatic source said.
"The United States has called time-out after the fighting," another Western envoy said. "President Clinton hopes both parties have stared into the abyss and will pull back."
Unprecedented gunbattles between Israeli soldiers and Palestinian police last week killed 72 people, 57 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers.

The fighting erupted after Netanyahu, in office for just 100 days at the head of a right-wing coalition, opened an entrance from Arab Jerusalem's Moslem quarter into an archaeological tunnel near Islam's third holiest shrine.
Israeli defence chiefs have said they were not properly consulted about the opening, the implications of which the Shin Bet security service said it underestimated.
Europeans, Arabs and Moslem states as well as Israeli opposition parties have called the move a political blunder.

Netanyahu's critics say that he has undermined the 1993 Oslo peace accord with the PLO on Palestinian self-rule, halted the normalisation of relations with Arabs states, and cast a shadow over the economic benefits Israel hoped to reap from regional peace.
Netanyahu, in combative mood, went to Washington adamant that he would not reseal the tunnel.
"What I'd like to see is two things, first a cessation of violence and second a speedy resumption of negotiations and their conclusion," he told reporters on his plane.
Netanyahu offered to hold "continuous negotiations" on Hebron, the West Bank city in which Israeli soldiers should have redeployed seven months ago.
Arafat, too, spelled out his hopes.
"We are committed to concrete results. We hope something will be achieved," he told reporters on his way to the summit.
Beyond appearing on the same stage, it is difficult to see what other achievements the two-day summit will bring, analysts said.
Such thinking prompted Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, a key player in regional peacemaking, to boycott the meeting.
Arafat and Netanyahu are in a stand-off over the tunnel. If Netanyahu backs down he will lose credibility with his right-wing.

If Arafat backs down he will throw away one of the strongest cards in his hand. The tunnel has combined politics and religion, gaining Arafat support in impoverished Palestinian towns and refugee camps disillusioned with Oslo, and resonating throughout the Moslem world.

The two sides are also far apart on Hebron. Netanyahu argues that last week's violence validates his demands for new security arrangements in the disputed city. Arafat says a deal is deal, insisting that Netanyahu honour agreements signed by the previous Labour government and set a date for redeployment.
The stakes are also high for Clinton, who does not want to see the peace process, the jewel in his foreign policy crown, collapse five weeks before the presidential election.

Analysts and officials on both sides are loathe to write the obituary of the peace process which has survived the massacre of Arabs in Hebron by a Jew, and the slaughter of Jews in Israel by Moslem suicide bombers.
But they all agree that Oslo, after last week's battles, is looking pretty sick.
